brief.head: Too rich to glow
brief.text: Light stops track­ing in­come near the top, Ajay Shah said. Double the in­come of some­one at “the zenith of human pros­per­ity” and the light­ing will not dou­ble. {116-J03}

brief.head: Don’t tell Trump
brief.text: NASA and NOAA give their data away free. Say it softly, Ajay Shah warned: if Donald Trump watches the show, he will com­plain the US is not being com­pen­sated. {116-J07}

brief.head: Flaring up
brief.text: Russia burns off a lot of gas, Ajay Shah said, call­ing it a “pe­tro­leum pro­duc­ing coun­try which also hap­pens to have nu­clear weapons”. An ef­fi­cient pro­ducer wastes none. {116-J10}

brief.head: Taiwan, take note
brief.text: Ukraine’s deep strikes hold a les­son, Ajay Shah said. If China in­vades Taiwan, ex­pect hun­dreds of kilo­me­tres of the Chinese coast fac­ing it to get the same treat­ment. {#taiwan}

lead.kicker: Ajay Shah reads a wartime economy from space
lead.head: Russia’s economy, lit from above

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 116

body: Every night at 1:30 AM, American satel­lites pho­to­graph the Earth. Ajay Shah used those pic­tures to take on what he called one of the great­est ques­tions of the age: what shape is the Russian econ­omy in?
The an­swer, from a new paper by Shah and his col­leagues, is that it has barely moved. Comparing January with January, Russia’s lights in 2025 were about where they had been in 2019. {#flat}
## A glow that grows

The field began by ac­ci­dent. US gov­ern­ment satel­lites were pho­tograph­ing the world at night for un­re­lated pur­poses, Shah said, and “clever an­a­lysts started see­ing that by mis­take you were pick­ing up the light over cities”. As a city pros­pered, its foot­print of light grew.
The idea is easy to love. “Look at the world at night,” Shah said. “And if there is a suc­cess­ful human so­ci­ety down there, it will have lit up the place with light.”
Streetlights, cars and all-night petrol pumps rise with pros­per­ity. So Bandra West glows brighter than Bandra East, and North Korea is dark be­side South Korea.
## Handle with care

But Shah, trained at CMIE never to use a mea­sure ca­su­ally, spent much of the hour on its traps. Nighttime lights, he now says, is far away from GDP: it is a proxy for eco­nomic ac­tiv­ity. {116-C02}

Testing the data on places they knew, his team found Bombay’s ra­di­ance col­laps­ing every July. The few mon­soon nights classed as cloud-free, they rea­soned, still car­ried wisps of cloud that dimmed the sig­nal. {116-S03}
Their fix was de­lib­er­ately con­ser­va­tive: cor­rect only where they were ab­so­lutely sure, so that ev­ery­one could safely adopt it.
## Enter Russia

Then came Russia. A long war, Shah ar­gued, is a war of eco­nom­ics, won by who­ever can keep pro­duc­ing guns, but­ter and sol­diers. Ukraine has Europe be­hind it. Russia, an Italy-sized econ­omy, has one im­por­tant pa­tron: North Korea.

Shah, Susan Thomas and Ayush Patnaik held off for years, sure that one of some 500 ca­pa­ble labs would do it. No good paper on Russia ap­peared. Then, in 2024, Swedish in­tel­li­gence said Russia’s lights had fallen sharply in 2023, and the team de­cided to do the work them­selves. {116-S04}

Russia broke meth­ods built for India. At 1:30 AM on a sum­mer night in St Petersburg, the sun is shin­ing. Moonlight over the vast­ness of Siberia added up to false ra­di­ance, and the Aurora Borealis lit up Ukraine in 2019.

The find­ings: war pro­duc­tion up, the civil­ian econ­omy down, the total about flat. Regions near Ukraine are hit by deep strikes, and those near the Baltic states by sanc­tions. The east is doing fine.
The economy’s cen­tre of mass, Shah said, has moved 245 kilo­me­tres east. {116-C10}
Shah now waits for January 2026, when Donald Trump’s eas­ing of sanc­tions and Ukraine’s im­prov­ing deep-strike weapons will pull in op­po­site di­rec­tions.
Amit Varma, moved to verse three times in the episode, pro­posed the next topic: other un­con­ven­tional ways of mea­sur­ing how a so­ci­ety lives.

second.label: The Second World War
second.head: Poking the giant
second.deck: Ajay Shah on why the Second World War was decided by production

pic.caption: USS Shaw explodes during the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor in 1941

body: When Japan at­tacked Pearl Harbor and “poked the giant”, Hitler fool­ishly de­clared war on America the very next day, Ajay Shah said. Hitler thought he was obliged to. He did not un­der­stand America. {116-J17}

Once American pro­duc­tion was mo­bilised, Shah ar­gued, the war was de­cided. Japan, an is­land, needed raw ma­te­ri­als from across East Asia, and the US Navy stran­gled its sup­ply chains. Occupied Europe could not match the US, Britain with its em­pire, and the Soviet Union com­bined. {116-S06}

Battles still mat­tered: D-Day could have been lost. But in a long strate­gic war, Hitler could not com­pete. Amit Varma doubted any­one un­der­stands America even now. “I don’t think America un­der­stands America,” he said. {116-J08}

quote.text: And when American pro­duc­tion was mo­bi­lized on one side, it was re­ally game over.

third.head: The poster he wouldn’t use

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the poster on the office wall

body: At NIPFP, Ajay Shah’s col­leagues Shekhar Hari Kumar and Shubho Roy were pas­sion­ate en­thu­si­asts of night­time lights. They made beau­ti­ful maps, and a poster went up in the of­fice.

Shah held back for years. Trained at CMIE, he said, you don’t ca­su­ally jump into using data: “Either I will have ex­treme mas­tery on un­der­stand­ing the in­nards and the dif­fi­cul­ties and the lim­i­ta­tions and the trust­wor­thi­ness of a mea­sure, or I will not use it at all.” {116-S02}
He dived in only when Ayush Patnaik began work­ing in­side the VIIRS data with great in­ten­sity and ef­fort.
Many econ­o­mists, he said, sim­ply take the World Bank’s file, which cov­ers all 671 dis­tricts of India, and hope “that noth­ing is bad”. {#districts}

box.title: The paper behind the episode
box.text: *Shedding Light on the Russia-Ukraine War*, by Rounak Hande, Ayush Patnaik, Ajay Shah and Susan Thomas, reads Russia’s econ­omy from cor­rected night­time lights. Its meth­ods paper, *But Clouds Got In My Way*, nods to Joni Mitchell’s *Both Sides Now*. {116-J15}

sections.label: The idea
sections.head: The Koreas, after hours
sections.caption: the Korean peninsula at night
body: Nighttime lights began as a by-product, Ajay Shah said: satel­lites pho­tograph­ing the Earth for un­re­lated pur­poses turned out to be pick­ing up the glow of cities, and that glow grew as cities pros­pered.

He showed the field’s most iconic pic­ture, North and South Korea at night in 2012 and again in 2025, and called it “one of the most in­flu­en­tial pic­tures in the his­tory of the so­cial­ism ques­tion”. {116-J16}

Answer one to that ques­tion, he said, was Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn’s *One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich*. The pho­to­graph was an­swer two. Socialism, he added, should have been tried on ham­sters first. {116-R04}
## Free to the world

NASA, NOAA and the European and Japanese space agen­cies re­lease well-maintained data free to the world, and keep up­dat­ing it as mis­sions run for ten or twenty years. “This is re­ally glo­ri­ous,” Shah said. It is mea­sure­ment with­out the in­sti­tu­tional com­plex­ity of a sta­tis­tics of­fice walk­ing the coun­try. {116-C03}

Because each pixel is small, any bound­ary can be drawn. His team has added up the light of 300 urban local bod­ies in Karnataka, a city-level mea­sure that tra­di­tional sta­tis­tics can­not match. {#karnataka}
The data is also monthly, where GDP comes out once a year with a long lag.
~ The re­al­ity, Shah warned, is more trou­ble­some: “There’s many a slip be­tween cup and lip.”

quote.text: These are pub­lic goods being pro­duced using gov­ern­ment money. So it is a sta­tis­ti­cal sys­tem with a twist.

sections.label: The catches
sections.head: Moonlight over Jaisalmer
sections.caption: the limits of the data
body: Ajay Shah walked through what the satel­lite sees. A for­est is dark, and so is the sea, ex­cept for ships: a clus­ter of them wait­ing at a port re­veals con­ges­tion. {#ships}
At 1:30 AM a pros­per­ous place has street­lights, com­pound walls, cars on roads and all-night restau­rants. So Bandra West is brighter than Bandra East, and the data shows it.
## Where the light lies
Then come the catches. Go from a one-storey build­ing to a five-storey one, Shah said, and the light does not re­ally in­crease up there: the roofs trap it. {#storey}
A town that switches to LEDs looks as if it has dimmed. LEDs de­liver about 34 per cent less light to the sen­sor, be­cause much of what they emit does not get through the at­mos­phere. {#led}
Thick clouds can blot out whole nights; in a July in Maharashtra, al­most no light comes through.
On moon­lit nights, faint light bounces off empty ground. Added up over an area as big as Jaisalmer, it can match Bandra West, whose GDP is ten times big­ger.
~ And near the top, lights stop ris­ing with in­come: Switzerland and the United States prob­a­bly look much the same. Economists, Shah said, got a bit over-excited.

quote.text: Nighttime lights is far away from GDP. It’s a proxy for eco­nomic ac­tiv­ity.

sections.label: The method
sections.head: Garbage in, garbage out
sections.caption: measuring before theorising
body: Half the bat­tle in eco­nom­ics, Ajay Shah said, is mea­sur­ing some­thing cor­rectly. The anal­y­sis and the­o­ris­ing come after. Without depth in mea­sure­ment, “you’ll just end up doing garbage in, garbage out, and we’re wast­ing everybody’s life”. {116-C04}
His first test of any dataset is places he knows. Is Bandra West brighter than Bandra East? Is Bandra East brighter than Karjat? If not, “there is some gol­maal, some­thing is amiss.” {116-C05}
## The July prob­lem

The test turned up a puz­zle: Bombay seemed to go dark every July. NASA and NOAA drop cloudy nights and av­er­age the rest, and in July only about three of 31 pass. Shah’s team rea­soned that those nights still car­ried wisps of cloud. {116-S03}

The frac­tion of cloud-free days, then, could mea­sure the bias. They built a de­lib­er­ately con­ser­va­tive cor­rec­tion, choos­ing to un­der­cor­rect so that ev­ery­one could adopt it safely and leave bolder fixes to later re­searchers. {116-C06}
Checked else­where, it barely changed cloud­less Dubai, and added value in cities like Johannesburg, which has a mon­soon in part of the year.
~ The paper and a Julia pack­age are pub­lic. Amit Varma praised the de­ci­sion to let any­one play with the data and change its pa­ram­e­ters: “That’s a spirit of in­quiry.”

quote.text: So we un­der­cor­rect, but we are ab­so­lutely sure that we are adding value by our un­der­cor­rec­tion.

art.caption: Ajay Shah on measuring before theorising

sections.label: The war economy
sections.head: More guns, less butter
sections.caption: strategic war as economic war
body: A long war, Ajay Shah ar­gued, is a bat­tle of economies. Bravery and gen­er­als mat­ter, but the econ­omy has to pro­duce the guns, the but­ter and the able-bodied sol­diers. {116-C07}
Ukraine need not pro­duce much. It is backed by Europe, where the guns are made in Germany and the but­ter in the UK. Russia, an Italy-sized econ­omy, has one im­por­tant pa­tron: North Korea.
## Four blows

Shah listed the pres­sures on Russia. One to two mil­lion of its most ed­u­cated and rich­est peo­ple fled. Western sanc­tions made buy­ing, pay­ing and earn­ing hard. The econ­omy was re­jigged to­wards war pro­duc­tion. {116-C08}

Fourth, and new­est, are Ukraine’s stand­off weapons. In the Second World War, Soviet fac­to­ries moved deep in­land were safe, be­cause Germany never built a long-range bomber. Today Ukraine can hit tar­gets up to 2,000 kilo­me­tres in­side Russia, more than the dis­tance from Delhi to Bangalore. {#bangalore}
“So imag­ine there’s a war going on at Delhi,” Shah said. “But there are deep strike weapons com­ing and hit­ting near the Karnataka Tamil Nadu bor­der.” {116-C09}
~ These weapons, he said, ar­rived only in the last six to nine months; the hosts were speak­ing in August.

quote.text: First, we’ve al­ways known that strate­gic war is a war of eco­nom­ics.

sections.label: The findings
sections.head: The economy heads east
sections.caption: Russia’s lights, January to January
body: Russia has pulled back on re­leas­ing data, Ajay Shah said, “as they should, be­cause that data is strate­gic”. Satellites fill the gap.
He com­pares January with January. Russian Januaries are dark at 1:30 AM and free of cloud: “January is the time to peek into the Kremlin.” {116-J09}
War pro­duc­tion is up and the civil­ian econ­omy down. Put to­gether, Shah said, from 2019 to 2025 “the quick an­swer is about zero change.” {#flat}
## A map in red
On his map of prov­inces, the re­gions around the Ukraine bor­der are deep red. Ukraine’s stand­off weapons, Shah said, are hit­ting deep in­side Russia.

Regions bor­der­ing the Baltic states have suf­fered from sanc­tions, as the gains from trade went into re­verse. The east­ern bor­ders, where sanc­tions are prob­a­bly not being en­forced, have done rea­son­ably well.
Net net, the cen­tre of mass of the Russian econ­omy has moved 245 kilo­me­tres east. {116-C10}
Amit Varma had one last idea: an episode on un­con­ven­tional met­rics, such as ris­ing di­vorce rates as a sign that women are em­pow­ered. {116-C11}
~ Shah is now watch­ing for January 2026: Donald Trump eas­ing sanc­tions, against Ukraine im­prov­ing its deep-strike weapons.

quote.text: So the Russian econ­omy is shift­ing in its char­ac­ter away from the west to the east.

art.caption: Ajay Shah on Russia’s lights, January to January

quote.text: I think that’s the core in­tel­lec­tual hon­esty of being a good econ­o­mist, which is you must be pas­sion­ate about mea­sure­ment. You have to re­ally wage war on mea­sure­ment.

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the month Bombay vanished from the satellite
stories.head: Monsoon, with a chance of bias
body: Ajay Shah and his col­leagues began their work on night­time lights the way he says ev­ery­one should: by check­ing the data against places they knew. Is Bandra West brighter than Bandra East? Does the light of Bombay add up? {116-C05}
When they plot­ted the graphs, some­thing jumped out. Bombay’s ra­di­ance seemed to col­lapse every July. {116-S03}

That made no sense. “We know there is ab­so­lutely no de­cline of the GDP of Bombay or the eco­nomic ac­tiv­ity in Bombay every July,” Shah said. July is the mon­soon, so clouds were the ob­vi­ous sus­pect, but NASA and NOAA say they work only on cloud-free days.

So the team dug into the method. Each night the satel­lite takes a pic­ture at 1:30 AM. A sep­a­rate step clas­si­fies it, zero or one, as cloudy or clear. Cloudy nights are thrown away and the rest av­er­aged. Over a pixel in Bombay, that might leave three nights in July.

Two ideas cracked it. The first: “We are from Bombay. We know that there are no cloud free days in July in Bombay.” The sec­ond: if a month has 28 cloudy days and three clear ones, the clear ones prob­a­bly carry wisps of cloud, enough to dim the light.
That made the frac­tion of cloud-free days a mea­sure of the bias. January, when 25 nights of data out of 31 come through, is gen­uinely clear; July, with three, is not. {#january}

~ They built an ex­tremely con­ser­va­tive cor­rec­tion and tested it abroad. In Dubai, cloud-free all year, it barely changed any­thing. In Johannesburg, where there is a mon­soon for part of the year, it added value.
stories.why: Great in­sti­tu­tions can miss a bias that local knowl­edge ex­poses at once. The clue was some­thing any Bombay res­i­dent knows: the city is never re­ally clear in July. {116-S03}
stories.postscript: The paper and a Julia pack­age are pub­lic. There is no case, Shah said, for any­one to keep using the un­cor­rected data.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Bombay’s dark Julys

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the surprises of studying the biggest country
stories.head: Sunshine at 1:30 in the morning
body: Russia, Ajay Shah found, breaks meth­ods built for India. It is so big that his team strug­gled to load its satel­lite im­agery into a computer’s mem­ory. They cut it into prov­inces, and the big­gest is still big­ger than India. {#province}
The satel­lites pho­to­graph the Earth at 1:30 AM. “You’ll be pleased to know that in the sum­mer at one thirty AM in Saint Petersburg, the sun is shin­ing,” Shah said. {116-S05}

Then there was Siberia. Little dribs of moon­light re­flect­ing off its empty vast­ness added up to what looked like real ra­di­ance. The team’s back­ground-noise al­go­rithms had been tuned for the deserts of Rajasthan, which are small by com­par­i­son.
~ Gas flares had to be fil­tered out too, and in 2019 the Aurora Borealis pro­duced an amaz­ing amount of light over Ukraine.
stories.why: Methods tuned for one coun­try can fail badly in an­other. Shah’s team caught each trap only by stay­ing close to the data, which is why he told every econ­o­mist to love their data deeply. {116-J13}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Russia’s midnight sun

stories.kicker: Why Swedish intelligence beat the academics to Russia
stories.head: Spies got there first
body: When the war began, Ajay Shah wanted to study Russia with night­time lights. He, Susan Thomas and Ayush Patnaik held back: it was too ob­vi­ous, some 500 labs knew the data, and surely the Europeans would do it. {#labs}

So they went back to house­holds in Karnataka. No good pa­pers on Russia’s econ­omy ap­peared, and the idea, Shah said, kept wak­ing up every three days. Then in 2024 Swedish in­tel­li­gence said Russia’s lights had fallen sharply in 2023. “Intelligence agen­cies in ad­vanced economies are using night­time lights data and the damn aca­demics are not,” Shah said. {116-S04}
“They have skin in the game,” Amit Varma said. Shah agreed, and drew the les­son: “you want to get some­thing done, do it your­self.”
~ It was a strug­gle, he ad­mit­ted: the team is grossly under-resourced. But they de­cided to do it any­way.
stories.why: Don’t as­sume an ob­vi­ous piece of re­search is al­ready being done. People who need an an­swer to act, like in­tel­li­gence agen­cies watch­ing a war, can out­run peo­ple who only need it to pub­lish.

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on how a field was born by mistake
stories.head: Born of a happy accident
body: The satel­lites were never meant for eco­nom­ics. US gov­ern­ment satel­lites were pho­tograph­ing the world at night for un­re­lated pur­poses, Ajay Shah said, when an­a­lysts no­ticed they were pick­ing up the light over cities. {116-S01}
Over the years, as a city suc­ceeded and grew, the foot­print of its light grew too. That led to a con­jec­ture: could light seen from space tell you about eco­nomic ac­tiv­ity?

The early data was crude: pix­els three kilo­me­tres across, the bright­est cities top-coded like audio that clips, read­ings once a year. Then, Shah said, came “a rev­o­lu­tion in 2011”, when NASA and NOAA launched the VIIRS sen­sors. {#revolution}
~ They pho­to­graph the world every night at 1:30 AM, in pix­els of about 700 to 800 me­tres, and the pic­tures are as­sem­bled into de­cent monthly sta­tis­tics.
stories.why: Whole re­search fields can grow from the by-products of some­one else’s project. The data was there all along; some­one just had to look at it with a dif­fer­ent ques­tion in mind.

quiz.q: What does the famous nighttime picture of the Korean peninsula answer, according to Ajay Shah?
quiz.a: Whether so­cial­ism works. It was an­swer two; Solzhenitsyn’s book was an­swer one.

quiz.q: Why did Bombay seem to go dark every July in the satellite data?
quiz.a: Its few ‘cloud-free’ mon­soon nights still car­ried wisps of cloud that dimmed the light.

quiz.q: Which month does Ajay Shah compare year on year to study Russia, and why?
quiz.a: January: Russian nights are dark at 1:30 AM and free of cloud.

quiz.q: How far east has the centre of mass of Russia’s economy moved?
quiz.a: 245 kilo­me­tres, as the west took strikes and sanc­tions and the east held up.

quiz.q: Why can’t a 1:30 AM photograph of summer St Petersburg count as night?
quiz.a: Because in sum­mer the sun is still shin­ing there at that hour.

quiz.q: Who said publicly in 2024 that Russia’s nighttime lights had fallen sharply in 2023?
quiz.a: Swedish in­tel­li­gence, which spurred Shah’s team to study Russia them­selves.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 116. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn (Bert Verhoeff for Anefo, CC0); Attack on Pearl Harbor (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Joni Mitchell (Library of Congress Life, CC0).

shelf.title: What Should India Do? (Episode 114)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: That episode ar­gued that deal­ing with America and China re­quires deep knowl­edge of them.

shelf.title: Metrics of Empowerment (Episode 88 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Three schol­ars in­vent un­con­ven­tional, in­tu­itive mea­sures of women’s em­pow­er­ment, from who or­ders the gro­ceries to women in pris­ons and solo travel, along­side Amit’s own: ris­ing di­vorce rates.

shelf.title: We Should Celebrate Rising Divorce Rates
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s provoca­tive ar­gu­ment that ris­ing di­vorce rates, often lamented as ‘be­com­ing like the West’, show more women gain­ing the agency and means to leave bad mar­riages.

laughs.text: Ajay on the North Korea vs South Korea night image as the an­swer to whether so­cial­ism works: ‘you should have tried it on ham­sters first.’
The word ‘incandescent’ sparks a qua­train from Amit: ‘I told her she was in­can­des­cent when I met her for a lark. She looked at me with twin­kling eyes and said I was too dark.’

Ajay’s pas­sion for mea­sure­ment in­spires an­other: ‘I said to her, I’ll trea­sure you, I love you bit by bit. But first, my love, I’ll mea­sure you to make sure that I fit.’ When Ajay says he’s get­ting bet­ter and bet­ter, Amit replies: ‘You weren’t a good econ­o­mist at twenty or thirty or forty, it took some time.’
Amit: ‘the rea­son you’re my fa­vorite econ­o­mist friend... Sorry to other econ­o­mist friends who might be watch­ing this, oh wait, I have none.’
The iconic satel­lite image of North and South Korea at night, shown for 2012 and 2025, which Ajay calls ‘one of the most in­flu­en­tial pic­tures in the his­tory of the so­cial­ism ques­tion.’

Pearl Harbor, where Japan ‘poked the giant’, fol­lowed by Hitler declar­ing war on America the next day. Ajay notes Hitler had no idea that ‘a MAGA iso­la­tion­ist prob­lem was alive and well in America at that time.’
